claims.text: An iterative machine-learned interatomic potential can substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The machine-learned potential can maintain fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
A sparse, representative set of ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations from both solid and liquid phases is sufficient to calibrate the potential.
Explicit correction schemes can retain anharmonic vibrational effects and electron–vibration coupling in the resulting free energies.
Accurate interpolation across diverse solid- and liquid-phase configurations preserves the structural and vibrational information required for free-energy evaluation.
Rapid machine-learned estimates of energies and forces reduce the amount of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling required.
Iterative training combined with entropy-related corrections will keep the solid and liquid free energies faithful to full ab initio results.
Phase free-energy differences, melting temperatures, and latent heats will be within approximately 5% of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The method will provide a 5–10× speedup relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method will be at least 2× faster than TOR-TILD for binary systems.
The method is initially applicable to elemental and binary systems near their melting points.
Application to multicomponent high-entropy alloys may require additional calibration because of their greater chemical complexity.
Small free-energy variations near melting significantly affect calculated fusion properties.
Prior elemental and binary results make the proposed approach promising.
Scalability to chemically complex multicomponent systems has not been validated.
